overview.text: A magnet is an object that produces a magnetic field—a region where magnetic forces act. Most familiar magnets have north and south poles: opposite poles attract, while like poles repel. Their fields can pull on certain materials, especially iron, cobalt, and nickel; magnets can also influence a nearby compass needle, which turns to align with Earth’s magnetic field. Magnets matter both as simple tools and as part of electromagnetism: a current flowing through a wire coil creates a magnetic field, making an electromagnet. Magnetic compasses have helped people navigate for centuries, using a freely turning magnetized needle to indicate direction.

key_facts.text: Opposite magnetic poles attract; like poles repel.
Iron, cobalt, and nickel are examples of materials whose atoms can have strong magnetic properties.
A magnetic compass works because its magnetized needle turns to align with Earth’s magnetic field.
Electric current produces a magnetic field; a coil of wire can use this effect to act as an electromagnet.
People have used magnetic compasses for navigation for hundreds of years.
